tytul: Grape juice from a steam juicer (UC Master Food Preservers)
wstep: This card describes the method of the University of California (UC) Master Food Preservers for canning grape juice made in a steam juicer, in a boiling-water bath.

sekcje.naglowek: Why the juice must be processed
akapity: UC warns that pouring steam-juicer juice straight into sterilized jars, capping them and storing them at room temperature without further processing (“bottling”) is not safe.
NCHFP: jars of fruit juice must be processed in a boiling-water canner long enough to destroy spoilage organisms.
According to UC, if you do not can the juice, keep it in the refrigerator for up to one week; for longer storage, freeze it.
According to UC, freeze juice in freezer-safe containers, such as metal or rigid plastic containers or glass jars, and leave headspace because juice expands when frozen.

For juice, NCHFP gives 1/2 inch (about 1.3 cm) of headspace for a pint and 1 inch (about 2.5 cm) for a quart in wide-mouth containers, and 1 1/2 inches (about 3.8 cm) for both sizes in narrow-top containers.
UC recommends straight-sided glass jars for freezing, to help prevent breakage.
According to UC, use good-quality fruit that is ripe but not overripe, and throw out any damaged or moldy fruit.
UC recommends not using windfall fruit, which has fallen to the ground, for juice or for canning.
Extract the juice according to your steam juicer’s instructions; if necessary, strain it through a sieve or cheesecloth to remove seeds.
In a clean, non-reactive saucepan, heat the juice just to a boil, with sugar to taste if you like, stirring until the sugar dissolves.
UC allows 5 minutes for half-pint and pint jars at 0–1000 ft only if the jars were sterilized first.
NCHFP puts the empty jars right side up on the rack in a boiling-water canner and fills the canner and jars with hot (not boiling) water to 1 inch (about 2.5 cm) above the tops of the jars.
To sterilize empty jars, NCHFP boils them for 10 minutes below 1000 ft, and above that 1 minute longer for each additional thousand feet.
JarAtlas rule for metres: boil the jars for 10 minutes up to 300 m, and add 1 minute for every further 300 m or part of it.
Just before filling, remove and drain the hot sterilized jars one at a time.
According to UC, ladle the hot juice into hot jars, leaving 1/4 inch (about 0.6 cm) of headspace.
Wipe the rims with a damp, clean paper towel or cloth, put on the lids and screw the bands on only fingertip-tight.
According to UC, at 0–1000 ft (up to 300 m) process half-pint and pint jars for 5 minutes, but only if they were sterilized first, and quart jars for 10 minutes.
If the half-pint or pint jars were not sterilized, UC gives no time for them at this elevation, so sterilize them first as described above.
Above 1000 ft the food may spoil if the time is not increased.
According to UC, at 1001–6000 ft (above 300 m up to 1800 m) process half-pints and pints for 10 minutes and quarts for 15.
According to UC, above 6000 ft (above 1800 m) process half-pints and pints for 15 minutes and quarts for 25.
The card converts feet to metres and rounds the limits down, towards the longer time: 1000 ft becomes 300 m and 6000 ft becomes 1800 m.
Shortening the time or cooling jars in cold water can also lead to spoilage.
The NCHFP Grape Juice recipe (juice from crushed, cooked grapes) gives quarts the same time as pints; for steam-juicer juice UC gives quarts longer times, and JarAtlas uses the UC times.
These times are for US jar sizes: a pint holds about 473 ml and a quart about 946 ml.
JarAtlas rule (the source does not test metric jars): for a jar of up to 473 ml use the pint time, and for a larger jar of up to 946 ml, for example 0.5 l or 0.9 l, use the quart time.
UC also allows half-gallon jars for grape juice, only in a boiling-water canner; this card does not describe them, and JarAtlas recommends jars of up to 946 ml.
According to UC, after processing, turn off the heat, remove the canner lid and wait 5 minutes before taking the jars out.
When you take the hot jars out of the canner, do not retighten the lids or bands; this can cut through the gasket and cause seal failures.

Cool the jars at room temperature for 12 to 24 hours, then remove only the screw bands (the metal rings of two-piece lids), leaving the flat lids on the jars, and test the seal: press the middle of the lid, and if it springs up when you release it, the jar is not sealed.
A sealed lid is concave, curved down slightly in the centre; if the centre is flat or bulging, the jar may not be sealed.
If a jar has not sealed at this check, keep it in the refrigerator and eat it within several days.

Store sealed jars in a clean, cool, dark, dry place, not above 95 °F (35 °C) and not near hot pipes, a stove or a furnace, in an uninsulated attic or in direct sunlight; in such conditions the food may spoil.
Before using a stored jar, check that the lid is tight and holds a vacuum: a good seal has a concave centre.
Look for streaks of dried food running from the top of the jar, rising air bubbles and unnatural colour.
When opening the jar, check for an unnatural smell, spurting liquid and cotton-like mould on the food or under the lid.
Do not taste food from a jar with an unsealed lid or with signs of spoilage.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): throw out such a jar.
